tooltip.description: Describes someone who pursues relationships for money, first noted in the Roaring Twenties.
Coined to name Clara Bow as the era’s ultimate style and charm icon.
Popularized by The Saturday Evening Post, it meant calling something pure nonsense.
The male counterpart to “It Girl,” labeling a young man with instant sex appeal.
Derived from “bookish,” it labeled anyone known for loving books in the early ’30s.
Captured the flash and flair of early-Hollywood style—something eye-catching and cool.
A playful onomatopoeia that quickly became the casual term for belching.
Celebrated the end of Prohibition—being seriously drunk was “beered up.”
From vaudeville and early comedy, a “boffo” show was one that got roaring laughter.
A cheeky term for grandpa—or any older fellow who seemed out of touch.
Named after the popular game halls springing up when entertainment was king.
Slang for something slimy or gross—think of early special-effects movies.
Short for “favorite,” it moved from Hollywood write-ups into everyday chatter.
Originally described athletes trash-talking opponents before games.
Label for postpartum sadness, coined when parenting magazines took off.
Called out a handsome heartthrob—Cary Grant epitomized being a “dreamboat.”
Short for “hyperactive,” used to describe overly energetic kids in wartime America.
Surprisingly first used in a 1940s cartoon—our go-to for “Well, no kidding!”
From military slang for a secondary bomb to meaning someone who crashes your plans.
Originally from a popular radio show—Homer Simpson’s catchphrase came decades later.
To be “cheesed off” was to be seriously annoyed—right alongside slang like “square.”
Meant someone pretentious or overly boho—think Edith Head’s wild costume creations.
From government lingo for the Federal National Mortgage Association to student loan slang.
To be in the “Jet Set” meant living the glamorous, globe-trotting life of postwar elites.
Hollywood coined this for its glamorous stars; soon everyone used it for “the in crowd.”
First printed in Newsweek as a synonym for “square”—never a compliment.
Described a grimy but loved watering hole—New Yorker articles popularized it.
Predated the ’60s: early beatniks used it to label bohemians chasing freedom.
“Boonies” meant remote countryside—often heard in WWII vets’ stories of home.
Embraced by jazz legends and James Dean—cemented as THE compliment.
Dubbed anyone obsessed with trivial details—usually the office micromanager.
Slang for something so great it’s like utopia—often used by jazz musicians.
Short for “nuclear bomb”—coined during the era of bomb tests and Cold War fears.
Surf culture’s term for showing off—thrill-seekers were true “hot-dogs.”
The opposite of Endsville—anything boring was “Dullsville.”
Baby boomers used it to call out annoying youngsters in early teen culture.
From fashion circles: calling someone or something gorgeous enough to stop traffic.
Originally military slang for goofing off—soon everyone used it for lame tasks.
Tom Wolfe’s Gatsby obsessed America made this faux-humble phrase a staple.
Meaning “gross,” it rode the wave of “groovy” culture before fading out.
College slang for a massive beer party—often in fraternities or backyards.
Jimi Hendrix declared “Let your freak flag fly,” embracing counterculture ideals.
Coined on Laugh-In to mean “rear end”—part of psychedelic-era lingo.
Used to call something unbelievably cool—jazz critics loved it first.
The ’70s kept “nerd” alive by labeling awkward folks as “dorky.”
Followers of the Grateful Dead embraced the name—still touring today.
As therapy grew, “guilt trip” captured the push to psychoanalysis.
Named after carbs—surfaced alongside the early Atkins and diet-culture boom.
Originally meant a bike fanatic—soon it was a legendary rock band’s name.
From early health-food movements to rehab jargon—“detox” did double duty.
Business execs adopted “hardball” to describe no-mercy negotiations.
Slang for beer—every college bar in America said “Pass the brewski.”
College life coined “pig-out” for epic junk-food binge sessions.
As Baby Boomers aged, anything retro became a “Nostalgia-Fest.”
With perms in vogue, “frizzy” labeled hair that didn’t cooperate.
Told to relaxation-resistant teens: “Take a chill pill, dude.”
“Buff” described a ripped physique—Arnold Schwarzenegger made it famous.
Started as a term for drum machines, then evolved into vocal percussion.
“Major” meant something huge or exciting—popularized by teen movies like Sixteen Candles.
Summed up the cool-factor of ’80s skate and surf culture.
A cheeky term for a charmingly handsome guy onscreen—Denzel Washington vibes.
Not the free stay-on-friends’-couches trend, but vegging out on the couch all day.
Emerging from Carlin’s notorious “7 dirty words,” dropping an F-Bomb shocked crowds.
NBA stars like Michael Jordan made “trash talk” a pre-game ritual.
A deliberately odd spelling of “cool,” championed by young skaters.
“Tighty Whiteys” referred to the classic snug underwear, featured in Risky Business.
Made infamous by Wayne’s World: add “NOT” at the end, and your statement flips.
Hip-hop tracks of the era used “Da Bomb” to praise something ridiculously awesome.
Biggie’s lyrics propelled “Benjamins” to symbolize $100 bills and wealth.
Popularized by Clueless, “As If!” let teens dismiss anything lame.
Teens everywhere shrugged with “Whatever,” cementing ’90s teen apathy.
Will Smith’s hit song turned “Jiggy” into a synonym for stylish swagger.
An acronym for “Pretty Hot And Tempting,” used to praise anything fresh and trendy.
Rap videos made “Bling” the ultimate badge of flashy success.
The Budweiser ad campaign made “Whassup?” the year’s most contagious greeting.
Described a close, nonsexual friendship—coined before Being John Malkovich made it trendy.
Bay Area kids used “hella” to mean “very”—soon West Coast slang went nationwide.
Naval term turned friend-group label—everyone’s “peeps” were their crew.
As low-rise jeans rose, showing that “muffin top” became a wardrobe hazard.
Snoop Dogg’s playful “Fo Shizzle” meant “for sure” in hip-hop circles.
“Sick!” praised something awesome—remains timeless in street-culture slang.
From tech demos to Twitter feeds, “GIF” sparked debates: “Jif” or “Gif”?
Slipped into pop culture when people started leaping into digital photos uninvited.
“Salty” described petty anger, especially over the smallest online slight.
Short for “as f*ck,” it gave maximum emphasis to any adjective with minimal effort.
“Before Anyone Else” gave couples a Twitter-friendly way to say “my boo.”
After the viral documentary, “catfish” meant an online romance built on lies.
When Netflix dropped full seasons, streaming marathons became “binge-watch.”
Memes made “shook” the go-to for being genuinely rattled or astonished.
Ghosting someone—vanishing without explanation—became a classic post-date move.
Originally drag slang for juicy gossip—everyone now spills the “tea.”
An epic, snappy rebuttal to trolls—Twitter wars made “clapback” famous.
Described awareness of social injustices—became a political and cultural rallying cry.
From an Eminem song to a dictionary entry—“stan” means superfan devotion.
To be overly dramatic or over-the-top—social media stars perfected “extra.”
“Cap” = lie; “No cap” = truth—became a staple on TikTok and Vine reboots.
Came from hip-hop to name anyone standing in your way—rivalries snapped coded.
Oxford added “rizz” in ’23 to label someone’s smooth game or charm.
TikTok users started testing “vibe check”: making sure the energy is on point.
Workers quitting hustle culture without leaving jobs made “quiet quitting” trend.
TikTok coined “goblin mode” for embracing lazy, unapologetically messy living.
Describes being overly self-referential online—born from social media introspection.
Astrology influencers labeled big life changes as “energy shifts” sweeping your sign.
